title: Characterizing quasiparticles in strongly correlated systems using nonlinear spectroscopy in quantum simulators
authors: Luka Skolc, Utso Bhattacharya, Jonathan B. Curtis, Immanuel Bloch, Eugene Demler
abstract: Characterizing carrier type in strongly correlated quantum systems conventionally relies on the Hall effect. In cold-atom quantum simulators, implementing Hall transport measurements typically requires synthetic gauge fields, which introduces significant heating. Here, we present nonlinear spectroscopic and fluctuation-based protocols that establish an alternative route to identifying the sign of quasiparticle charge. We demonstrate that second-order density and current responses to finite-momentum quenches and drives-as well as equilibrium third-order density cumulants-distinguish electron- from hole-like quasiparticles. For a Fermi-Hubbard multi-leg ladder on a square lattice, numerical simulations reveal a crossover from hole- to electron-like carriers upon hole-doping away from half-filling, matching the sign change in the Hall coefficient. To demonstrate the applicability of our protocols beyond fermionic systems, we show that the nonlinear density response to a finite-momentum, finite-frequency drive reveals the sign of charge carriers in a hard-core boson ladder, and that the nonlinear signal can be significantly enhanced when driving near resonance with a nonlinear collective mode. Our results establish nonlinear density and current response and equilibrium non-Gaussian fluctuations as complementary probes, offering quantum simulators a direct route to characterize the carrier sign, without the experimental hurdles of conventional transport setups.
summary: This work introduces nonlinear spectroscopic and fluctuation-based protocols to determine the sign of quasiparticle charge carriers in strongly correlated systems, bypassing the heating issues associated with traditional Hall measurements in quantum simulators. By analyzing second-order density responses and density skewness, the authors demonstrate a direct, complementary route to characterizing carrier type in models like the Fermi-Hubbard model. This offers quantum simulators a robust diagnostic tool for fundamental condensed matter questions.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of characterizing the sign of quasiparticle charge carriers in strongly correlated systems without relying on the conventional Hall effect, which is problematic in cold-atom quantum simulators due to heating.
main_result: Nonlinear spectroscopic responses (second-order density response) and equilibrium non-Gaussian fluctuations (density skewness) provide complementary, direct probes to determine the sign of the charge carriers, successfully reproducing known sign changes observed in the Hall coefficient.
method: The authors employ theoretical modeling combined with numerical simulations, utilizing nonlinear response functions ($\chi^{(2)}$) and higher-order cumulants ($C^{(3)}$) applied to quantum simulators.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Fermi-Hubbard Model (FHM), relevant to Mott physics and high-Tc cuprates. The methods are shown to be applicable to bosonic systems, such as hard-core bosons, in cold-atom quantum simulators.
key_observables: Second-order density response ($ho_2$), equilibrium density skewness ($C^{(3)}$), and the Hall coefficient ($R_H$).
important_parameters: Doping level (especially near half-filling), temperature ($T$), and interaction strength ($U/t$).
main_assumptions: The protocols assume single-site resolution is available, which is achievable in cold-atom quantum simulators, bypassing the need for complex transport measurements.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the sign determination via $ho_2$ and $C^{(3)}$ for both fermionic (FHM) and bosonic systems, showing crossovers matching expected physical transitions.
paper_structure: The paper develops the concept by first proposing nonlinear probes to replace the Hall effect. It then applies these methods to the FHM, demonstrating the sign change upon doping, and extends the methodology to bosonic systems using nonlinear spectroscopy.
why_interesting: It provides a powerful, experimentally viable diagnostic tool for strongly correlated physics in AMO platforms, linking measurable nonlinear optical/density responses directly to fundamental electronic properties like carrier type.
